findings.title: Untrusted pull-request code executes on self-hosted ARC runners
findings.what: Both workflows run for pull_request events on `arc-runner-set`, check out the pull request merge content, and then execute files controlled by that pull request. Even the preliminary docs-only jobs execute `scripts/ci-docs-only.mjs`; subsequent jobs run `npm ci` (including package lifecycle hooks), builds, tests, and other npm scripts. A malicious pull request can therefore execute arbitrary code on self-hosted runner infrastructure, potentially attacking runner persistence, accessible network services, or the surrounding cluster despite the read-only GitHub token.
findings.fix: Do not execute fork-controlled pull-request content on these self-hosted runners. Run pull-request validation on GitHub-hosted or equivalently isolated single-use runners with no sensitive network reach, or gate self-hosted execution to trusted same-repository branches after an explicit authorization step while ensuring the authorization logic itself runs trusted base-branch code.
findings.acceptance: Open a pull request from a fork that changes `scripts/ci-docs-only.mjs`, package lifecycle scripts, or an invoked npm script. Verify that no job executing the changed code is scheduled on `arc-runner-set`; trusted same-repository pull requests must still run the required checks on an appropriately isolated runner.
findings.verifyNote: A separate second pass re-read both event declarations, runner selections, checkout steps, and every execution step at baseline c8b98a29508b5eb7725c75a7e2a41dfa94c1feba. The trigger has no fork or trust restriction, and both workflows execute checked-out PR-controlled JavaScript before or during their main jobs. Read-only GitHub permissions reduce token impact but do not isolate the self-hosted host or network.
